name: Gao
info: Gao is a city on the eastern bank of the Niger River in Mali, occupied by about 700 CE, a trading centre of the trans-Saharan routes, the capital of the Songhai Empire under Sunni Ali, and now the capital of the Gao Region.

facts.founded: Digs at Gao-Saney show the site was occupied by roughly 700 CE, and by no later than the early 10th century the Songhay king based at Kukiya had moved to Gao Ancien.
facts.where: On the eastern bank of the River Niger at the junction with the Tilemsi valley, 320 km east-southeast of Timbuktu, in eastern Mali.
facts.known: The kingdom of Kawkaw of the Arabic geographers; trans-Saharan trade; the Zuwa and Sonni rulers; Sunni Ali's capital of the Songhai Empire; Ibn Battuta's visit in 1352-53; the Tomb of Askia; the medieval Arabic epitaphs of Gao-Saney
facts.today: Gao is a city in Mali and the capital of the Gao Region.

t: Gao was a centre of manufacturing, iron smelting and trade by about 700 CE, and Arabic writers of the 9th century described it as an important regional power.

It became part of the Mali Empire towards the end of the 13th century, regained its independence in the first half of the 15th century, and became the capital of the Songhai Empire under Sunni Ali, who ruled from 1464 to 1492.
After the Moroccan invasion of 1591 the invaders made Timbuktu their capital, and by 1854 Heinrich Barth found Gao a village of about 300 huts.
dyk: Gao and the nearby site of Gao-Saney have more than 100 medieval Arabic inscriptions, the oldest dated to 1042 CE, which record generations of kings and queens in the form of epitaphs.
ev: Gao-Saney is occupied as a centre of iron smelting, manufacturing and trade
Al-Khwarizmi makes the earliest written mention of Gao, already an important regional power
The Songhay king based at Kukiya moves to the site of Gao Ancien
Gao loses its independence and becomes part of the Mali Empire
Ibn Battuta visits Gao, then part of the Mali Empire, and stays a month
Sunni Ali Ber begins his rule and makes Gao the capital of the Songhai Empire
The Moroccan invasion collapses the Songhai Empire and Timbuktu becomes the capital
Heinrich Barth finds Gao reduced to a village of about 300 huts

sections.origins:
Gao stands on the eastern bank of the Niger River at the junction with the Tilemsi valley, 320 km east-southeast of Timbuktu. Archaeological digs at Gao-Saney show that the site was occupied by roughly 700 CE and was a centre of manufacturing, iron smelting and trade with areas as far away as Mesopotamia. Pottery from the mounds is similar to that found throughout the region, which indicates that Gao was part of a regional market sphere, and the local character of the ceramic, animal and plant remains suggests that Gao-Saney belonged to a broader indigenous cultural complex of the Niger River. Fragments of North African enamel ware, Andalusian chandelier ware and Islamic glass vessels were also recovered.

The evidence points to two settlements on the eastern bank: Gao Ancien, within the modern town and east of the Tomb of Askia, and Gao-Saney, about 4 km to the east. Imported pottery and glass suggest that Gao-Saney was occupied between the 8th and 11th centuries. At some point no later than the early 10th century the Songhay king based at Kukiya moved to the site of Gao Ancien, and the kings of this period belonged to a lineage known as Qanda. Arabic geographers called the town Kawkaw or Kuku. In the Tarikh al-Sudan, al-Sadi names a legendary founder of the Zuwa dynasty, Zuwa Alayman, who he claims came from Yemen to Kukiya.
sections.growth:
The earliest written mention of Gao is by al-Khwarizmi, who wrote in the first half of the 9th century, when Gao was already an important regional power. Around 872 al-Yaqubi described the kingdom of the Kawkaw as the greatest of the realms of the Sudan, to whose king all the other kingdoms owed allegiance. Ibn al-Faqih, writing about 903, mentioned a caravan route from Egypt to ancient Ghana by way of Kawkaw. According to Ibn Hawqal, writing about 988, that route was abandoned in the reign of Ibn Tulun (868 to 884) after bandits attacked some caravans and blown sand overwhelmed others, and a route through Sijilmasa and across the Sahara replaced it. The excavators suggest that local elites made use of long-distance trade rather than being created by it.

Gao stood highest under the Songhai Empire. By the end of the 16th century it controlled an empire of more than 1,400,000 km2. Leo Africanus, who visited between 1506 and 1510, saw a large town without a surrounding wall, full of rich merchants. The Tarikh al-fattash reports that a survey made in the reign of Askiya Al-Hajj (1582 to 1586) counted 7,626 houses, not including huts of straw. At an average of 6 people to a house this implies a population of about 45,000, which would make Gao one of the largest cities of West Africa at the time.
sections.rulers:
In the 10th century Gao was already Muslim by the accounts of Arabic writers. Al-Sadi lists 32 rulers of the Zuwa dynasty and states that in 1009 to 1010 the 15th of them, Zuwa Kusoy, was the first to convert to Islam. John Hunwick, among others, speculates that the first version of Islam there was Ibadism. Around 1079 to 1082 a Sanhaja Berber group, inspired by the Sunni Almoravids, took control of the area and left royal epitaphs in a cemetery at Gao-Saney. Whether these kings appear on the king lists of the Za dynasty in the chronicles is debated, and Dierk Lange proposes that they represent the founding of the Sonni dynasty.

Towards the end of the 13th century Gao lost its independence and became part of the expanding Mali Empire. Sometime in the 14th century Ali Kulun, the first ruler of the Sunni dynasty, rebelled, but the Malians regained control. In the first half of the 15th century Sunni Sulayman Dama threw off Malian rule. His successor Sunni Ali Ber (1464 to 1492) greatly enlarged the territory and established the Songhai Empire, with Gao as its capital. Askiya Muhammad I, the first ruler of the Askiya dynasty, ruled the town when Leo Africanus visited. After the Moroccan invasion of 1591 the invaders made Timbuktu their capital.
sections.life:
Al-Muhallabi, who died in 990, described Gao as two towns. The king lived in the town west of the river with his men and those he trusted, where a mosque stood and where he prayed, while the town on the eastern bank, which he called Sarnah, had markets and trading houses. The communal prayer ground lay between them. Al-Muhallabi wrote that the king and most of his people only pretended to be Muslims. Ibn Battuta, who spent a month in Gao in 1352 to 1353, called it one of the finest, biggest and most fertile cities of the Sudan, with plenty of rice, milk, chickens, fish and cucumbers, and recorded that its people bought and sold with cowries, as the people of Mali did. He left with a caravan that included 600 slave girls.

Leo Africanus found the town very civilised compared with Timbuktu, with bread, meat, melons, cucumbers, squash and rice in abundance, many wells of sweet water, and no wine or fruit. On market days large numbers of male and female slaves were sold in a square, and he gave the price of a girl of fifteen as about six ducats. Today the people of Gao mostly speak Koyraboro Senni, and they include Bozo, Fulani cattle keepers, Tuareg, Arabs and Bambara from western Mali. The city is divided into nine quartiers.
sections.crises:
Ibn Khaldun recorded that in 1374 to 1375 Mali fought a war over Gao against Berber Tuareg forces from Takedda, and the war devastated the city. It did not regain its former importance until the rise of the Songhai Empire. The Moroccan invasion of 1591 collapsed that empire, and the invaders chose Timbuktu as their capital, after which the importance of Gao declined. When Heinrich Barth visited in 1854 he found about 300 huts of matting in clusters. The inhabitants were very poor and owned only a few boats because they had no wood to build them, and the site of the ancient town was overgrown with Capparis decidua bushes.

On 31 March 2012, one day after the capture of Kidal, Malian military forces retreated from Gao's bases and the MNLA and Ansar Dine occupied the city. On 6 April the MNLA declared the region independent of Mali as Azawad. On 26 and 27 June 2012 fighting between the MNLA and the Movement for Oneness and Jihad in West Africa ended with the MNLA driven from the city. French warplanes bombed parts of Gao in January 2013, and French and Malian forces captured the city on 26 January 2013. On 18 January 2017 a suicide bomber drove a vehicle filled with explosives into a military camp near Gao and killed 77 people.
sections.legacy:
Gao left a body of writing that questions the claim that no indigenous written records survive from before the middle of the 17th century. Over 100 medieval Arabic inscriptions come from Gao and Gao-Saney, the oldest dated to 1042 CE, with poetry and the epitaphs of many generations of kings and queens. A letter from Askia Muhammad I, quoted in al-Maghili's reply, adds details of 15th-century social and economic life. The two 17th-century chronicles, the Tarikh al-Sudan and the Tarikh al-fattash, cover the Songhai period, though their accounts before the second half of the 15th century are likely to be less reliable.

The mosque-tomb of Askia Muhammad, built between 1493 and 1538 and listed by UNESCO as the Tomb of Askia, covered about 2500 m2 and had seven bays parallel to the qibla wall and a courtyard with a minaret 12 metres high. Excavations in Old Gao also uncovered a mosque of the early 10th century. Gao is today a city in Mali, the capital of the Gao Region and the largest town in the east of the country, and it is regarded as a Songhay cultural capital. The urban commune had 86,633 people at the census of 2009.

summary: Gao, on the Niger in eastern Mali, was occupied by about 700 CE and became a trading centre, then the capital of the Songhai Empire under Sunni Ali. It declined after the Moroccan invasion of 1591 and is now the capital of the Gao Region.
references: John O. Hunwick, Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire: Al-Sadi's Tarikh al-Sudan down to 1613 and other contemporary documents (Brill, 2003)
Nehemia Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali (Methuen, 1973)
P.F. de Moraes Farias, Arabic medieval inscriptions from the Republic of Mali: Epigraphy, chronicles and Songhay-Tuareg history (Oxford University Press, 2003)
notes: No separate history article exists for Gao in wp/; the city's own article alone was used.
START: no founding date; 700 used with circa true from 'occupied by roughly 700CE' at Gao-Saney.

Al-Muhallabi: the article places the king's town west of the river but its archaeological discussion puts Gao Ancien on the east bank; the article itself notes this tension. I reported al-Muhallabi's account as his. The east/west arrangement was not resolved.

Zuwa Kusoy's conversion 1009-1010 is al-Sadi's claim; the article also says Gao was Muslim in the 10th century and the lead says by end of 10th century the ruler was said to be Muslim, so dates of conversion are in tension; both attributed.
Unclear ethnic/dynastic relation of Za, Zuwa, Sonni (Lange v. long-established opinion): left to one sentence.
Article says Ali Kulun rebelled 'sometime in the 14th century'; Sunni Ali's accession given 1464 in text, ruled 1464-1492.
Population 86,633 'in 2009' kept with the census year as a lasting figure, not 'as of'. Date range for the Ibn Battuta visit given as 1352-53 in text; event labelled 1352.

Left out: climate, the Niger flood, roads, bridge, ferries, twin towns, the 2015 helicopter crash, the 2026 attack (undeveloped one line), the Askia Tomb's date 1495 (article gives 1495 in Sites and 1493-1538 in Mosques; I used 1493-1538 only), the Kankou Moussa mosque.
'Largest town in eastern Mali' from the article's Location section ('sprawling town is the largest in eastern Mali').
'Excavators suggest local elites made use of trade' paraphrases the article's 'local elites capitalized on and co-opted the opportunities offered by long-distance trade'.
